title: The Relative Effectiveness of Human Tutoring, Intelligent Tutoring Systems, and Other Tutoring Systems
abstract: This article is a review of experiments comparing the effectiveness of human tutoring, computer tutoring, and no tutoring. “No tutoring” refers to instruction that teaches the same content without tutoring. The computer tutoring systems were divided by their granularity of the user interface interaction into answer-based, step-based, and substep-based tutoring systems. Most intelligent tutoring systems have step-based or substep-based granularities of interaction, whereas most other tutoring systems (often called CAI, CBT, or CAL systems) have answer-based user interfaces. It is widely believed as the granularity of tutoring decreases, the effectiveness increases. In particular, when compared to No tutoring, the effect sizes of answer-based tutoring systems, intelligent tutoring systems, and adult human tutors are believed to be d = 0.3, 1.0, and 2.0 respectively. This review did not confirm these beliefs. Instead, it found that the effect size of human tutoring was much lower: d = 0.79. Moreover, the effect size of intelligent tutoring systems was 0.76, so they are nearly as effective as human tutoring.
explain_beginner: This review looked at studies that compared students who received tutoring with students who learned the same material without tutoring. People often assume human tutors are far better than computer programs. The review found this is not true. Human tutoring produced a moderate improvement, and computer tutoring systems designed to respond step by step produced almost the same improvement. This matters because it suggests schools may get similar learning benefits from software as from human tutors, which could make extra help available to more students at lower cost.
explain_business: Leaders often assume that only human tutors deliver strong learning gains and that software is a weak substitute. This review of comparison studies found otherwise. Human tutoring improved outcomes by a moderate amount, and intelligent tutoring systems achieved almost the same result. The practical implication is that software based tutoring can deliver learning benefits close to those of human tutors, likely at much lower cost and with easier scaling. This informs decisions about where to invest limited instructional budgets, suggesting that intelligent tutoring software deserves serious consideration alongside human tutoring programs.
explain_practitioner: The author reviewed experiments comparing human tutoring, computer tutoring, and instruction covering the same content without tutoring. Computer systems were grouped by interaction granularity: answer-based, step-based, and substep-based. Intelligent tutoring systems typically use step or substep interaction, while other systems use answer-based interfaces. The common belief was that finer granularity yields larger effects, with expected effect sizes of 0.3, 1.0, and 2.0 for answer-based systems, intelligent tutoring systems, and adult human tutors. The review did not confirm this. Human tutoring measured 0.79, and intelligent tutoring systems measured 0.76, nearly equal.
